sections.html:
Flathead County's seat and northwest Montana's biggest city, Kalispell counted 24,558 people in 2020. The elevation is 3,084 feet, with Flathead Lake roughly 7 miles south. Hospital work is the largest source of jobs, anchored by Logan Health Medical Center, and the ski and visitor trade around Whitefish Mountain Resort brings seasonal jobs. Expect buyers who live here year-round and others shopping for a second home.

Winter arrives around late October and lingers through March, cold and moderately snowy. Summer is hot and dry. Your roof holds snow for about five months and your furnace works hard, so buyers ask how old each one is. Look up the install dates before you list. Because summers run dry, a tidy yard and a well-kept exterior help at showings.

sections.h2: Property tax due dates and penalties
sections.html:
Flathead County's Treasurer bills and collects property tax in two installments. The office is at 290 A North Main in Kalispell, and the phone is 406-758-5680.

PaymentDue dateDelinquent after
First halfNovember 30December 1
Second halfMay 31June 1

A due date that falls on a weekend or holiday slides to the following business day, with payment accepted until 5:00 p.m. without penalty. Bills are mailed at least 30 days ahead of November 30. A late-mailed bill gives the taxpayer 30 days counted from its postmark.

sections.h2: Monthly payment plan for a primary residence
sections.html:
If the house is your primary residence, section 15-16-122 of the Montana Code lets you request an alternate schedule of seven monthly payments running from November 30 to May 31. The request must reach the county by September 30 of the taxing year, so asking in the fall is too late for that year's bill.

Sellers can use this to stay current while the house is listed. Any balance still open when the sale closes comes out of your proceeds.

sections.h2: How Montana values your home and sets the rate
sections.html:
The state revalues homes every two years at 100 percent of market value. Tax year 2025 uses three rate bands for a home: 0.76 percent on the first $400,000 of market value, 1.10 percent on value from $400,000 to $1.5 million, and 2.20 percent on anything above $1.5 million. Local levies sit on top of those bands, so the final bill depends on where your home's value lands.

Many buyers check the county's online tax lookup for a house they like. Open it yourself before choosing an asking price.

sections.h2: Short-term rental and accessory unit rules
sections.html:
The city and the county run separate systems, and that matters most if the house has been a vacation rental. City limits fall under the municipal code, which includes short-term residential rental standards and accessory dwelling unit provisions. Beyond the limits, Flathead County applies its own regulations.

In county terms, a short-term rental is a residential use of a dwelling designed for stays under 30 days. Most zoned areas call for an administrative conditional use permit. Reviews may take as long as six weeks and involve a notice to every owner within 150 feet. A few zones allow the use outright, others prohibit it, and unzoned land needs no Planning and Zoning permit.

Any buyer, cash or financed, will ask whether the permit exists and whether it passes to them. Call the planning office before listing, and put the permit paperwork in your sale folder.

sections.h2: What you must tell a buyer in Montana
sections.html:
Sellers hand the buyer a written statement of problems they know about. Topics include:

  • Anything clouding title or limiting your right to transfer.
  • Well, wastewater, septic and utility hookup trouble.
  • Defects in the structure, roof, foundation, plumbing, electrical or heating, plus water intrusion.
  • Building work done without a permit.
  • Pests, hazardous materials, soil or drainage issues, and results of any radon, mold, lead-based paint or contaminated soil testing.

Under section 70-20-502, the statement goes to the buyer before or with the contract. A late statement gives the buyer three days to back out under section 70-20-504, unless the buyer waived that right. Section 70-20-503 exempts court-ordered transfers, foreclosure sales, and transfers to a spouse, child or parent.

sections.h2: Ways to sell a Kalispell house
sections.html:
Three routes are open: an agent listing, a sale by owner, or a cash sale.

  • An agent listing reaches the most buyers. It also means showings, an inspection and a buyer who needs a loan.
  • Selling it yourself avoids a commission, though you carry the paperwork and the disclosure.
  • A cash sale has the buyer take the house as is, with no lender slowing things down. Price reflects the repairs and risk the buyer absorbs, so set the written offer beside your likely net from a listing before deciding.

Ask each buyer or agent how long they expect the process to take from signed contract to keys, and get that in writing.

sections.h2: Selling with taxes or a loan owed
sections.html:
Start with the money paperwork, whatever route you choose. Request a payoff statement from your lender. Write down any liens, back taxes or HOA dues before you sign. Taxes you still owe are paid out of the sale proceeds at closing, and the title company will ask the Treasurer for the exact amount.

Gather these before the first call with a buyer or agent:

  • Your latest property tax bill and any payment-plan paperwork.
  • The loan payoff statement.
  • Install dates for the roof and furnace.
  • Permits for additions, plus the short-term rental permit if you have one.
  • Notes on the well, septic or road access if the lot is rural.

• A rental house with an uncertain permit history.
  • Acreage where the well, septic or access needs explaining.
  • An inherited home split among relatives scattered across several states.
  • A job or family move with a hard deadline.
  • Delinquent taxes or a missed mortgage payment.

Most of these ease once the documents are in one folder. A cash sale skips the buyer's loan approval and lender appraisal, which can help when the calendar is tight.

faqs.q: When are Flathead County property taxes due?
faqs.a: The first half is due November 30 and the second half is due May 31. Unpaid amounts become delinquent on December 1 and June 1.

faqs.q: Can I pay my Kalispell property tax in monthly installments?
faqs.a: If it is your primary residence, you can ask the Flathead County Treasurer for seven monthly payments from November 30 to May 31. The request is due September 30 of the taxing year.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to rent my Kalispell house short term?
faqs.a: Most zoned parts of Flathead County require an administrative conditional use permit. Inside the city, check the municipal code or call the city's Development Services Department.

faqs.q: Do I have to disclose problems with my house in Montana?
faqs.a: Yes. Put in writing any adverse material facts you actually know, and deliver it before or with the contract. Some transfers, including court-ordered ones, are exempt.

faqs.q: Can a cash buyer close without an inspection or a loan?
faqs.a: With cash there is no lender, so no loan approval or bank appraisal. Whether the buyer inspects is something the two of you settle in the contract.
